en.title: Philosophy: the whole course
en.short: What philosophy is, how philosophy degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What philosophy is
sections.text:
Philosophy is the study of fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, reason, value, mind, language and society. It does not settle these questions by tradition or feeling alone. It builds and tests arguments: sets of reasons offered to support a conclusion. A philosophical claim is judged by how well it is argued, how clearly it is stated, and how it answers objections.

Philosophy matters because every field rests on assumptions. Science assumes that nature is orderly and that evidence matters. Law assumes ideas about responsibility and fairness. Ethics asks how we should live. Political philosophy asks what makes power legitimate. The subject trains you to examine assumptions, define terms and follow an argument wherever it leads.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degree structures differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BA Philosophy is commonly a four-year programme at many universities, though combined honours and other arrangements exist. In the United Kingdom, a BA is usually three years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and four in Scotland. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree is commonly four years. Master’s degrees are often one to two years, and doctorates three or more, but these patterns vary widely.

Awards include BA, MA, MPhil and PhD; some universities also use BPhil or other titles. Programmes usually combine compulsory foundation courses, optional specialist courses, tutorials or seminars, essays and examinations, and a final project or dissertation. Check your own handbook for length, credit units, required courses, assessment rules and regulations, because these change.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage starts with what philosophy is, logic and the analysis of argument, critical thinking and reasoning skills, and methods of philosophical inquiry. It then moves through early Greek philosophy, covering the Presocratics, Socrates and Plato; Aristotle and the Hellenistic schools; medieval, Islamic and early African thought; rationalism and empiricism; Kant’s response to them; and German idealism.

The core stage covers logic, language and the philosophy of science; phenomenology and existentialism; analytic philosophy of mind, meaning and ordinary language; African philosophy and its debates; metaphysics; free will, determinism and personal identity; philosophy of mind; epistemology; normative ethics and metaethics; applied and professional ethics; social and political philosophy; philosophy of religion; aesthetics; philosophy of law; philosophy of language; research methods and the philosophy essay; and African philosophy in the modern world.

At master’s level, the course turns to advanced metaphysics and mind, advanced epistemology and ethics, a dissertation in research design and writing, and a frontier topic on the philosophy of artificial intelligence and mind.

sections.heading: How to study philosophy
sections.text:
Read actively. For each text, identify the question, the thesis, the premises, the conclusion, the objections and the replies. Keep a glossary of technical terms and add your own examples. Do logic exercises regularly, because formal skills improve with practice.

Write essays as arguments, not summaries. State a thesis, defend it with reasons, raise the strongest objection you can, answer it, and cite your sources. Discuss ideas with classmates and test your reading against theirs. Use primary texts where possible, and check which translation or edition you are using. For African philosophy, read African authors and follow the debates about the nature of the field. Ask of every idea: what would count for it, and what would count against it?

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is treating philosophy as personal opinion. Opinion matters, but philosophy asks for reasons that others can examine. Another mistake is writing a history of views without answering the question. Students also name-drop philosophers without stating their arguments, ignore the best objection, or use terms such as idealism, empiricism and relativism loosely.

Some assume that one tradition, usually European, is universal and ignore African and other traditions. Others rely on summaries or chatbots and do not check claims. Plagiarism and missing citations are serious academic offences. Finally, do not force a simple answer where the question is contested. Show the disagreement fairly and explain why it remains.

keyPoints: Philosophy is the reasoned study of fundamental questions, not a collection of personal opinions.
A philosophy degree usually combines history of philosophy, logic, core areas and a dissertation, but length and awards vary by country and institution.
Learn each view as a set of premises, objections and replies.
Write essays that argue for a thesis and answer objections, not just summarise.
Name the country and period when discussing a philosopher or a rule.
Check your own handbook and use primary texts where possible.

en.title: What Is Philosophy?
en.short: Philosophy as critical study of fundamental questions, its branches and its method of argument.

sections.heading: Defining philosophy
sections.text:
Philosophy is the critical and systematic study of fundamental questions about knowledge, reality, values and reasoning. Critical means it tests claims with reasons rather than accepting them because they are traditional or popular. Systematic means it builds connected lines of thought, not isolated remarks. A question is fundamental when it lies beneath ordinary enquiries: not which medicine works, but what counts as evidence; not which act is legal, but whether law and morality coincide.

A short case shows the difference. Two students, Amina and Tunde, in Ibadan disagree about whether a person can be obliged to obey an unfair law. One says, “My father says so.” The other asks what obligation means, whether consent creates it, and what follows if it is broken. The second is doing philosophy.

sections.heading: The main branches
sections.text:
Metaphysics asks what exists and what it is like: minds, matter, time, causation. Epistemology asks what knowledge is, how we get it and when belief is justified. Ethics asks how we should act and what makes a life good. Logic studies the form of correct reasoning: when premises support a conclusion. Aesthetics asks about beauty, art and taste.

These are not separate boxes. A claim about free will (metaphysics) depends on what counts as evidence (epistemology). A judgement that a painting is good (aesthetics) may rest on reasons that ethics or metaphysics examines.

sections.heading: Argument, not opinion
sections.text:
Philosophy proceeds by argument: giving reasons that others can examine, and answering objections. An opinion is a belief held without supporting reasons. An argument is a set of premises offered as support for a conclusion. Philosophy does not ignore experience or tradition, but it asks them to justify themselves.

In the case above, “My father says so” is an appeal to authority. It may be true, but it is not yet a philosophical argument. The second student asks for premises that others could test. That demand for reasons is what makes philosophy critical and systematic.

keyPoints: Philosophy is the critical and systematic study of fundamental questions about knowledge, reality, values and reasoning.
Its main branches are metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic and aesthetics.
Metaphysics asks what exists; epistemology asks about knowledge; ethics asks about action and the good life.
Logic studies correct reasoning, and aesthetics studies beauty, art and taste.
The branches connect: claims in one area depend on assumptions examined in another.
Philosophy uses argument, not mere opinion: it gives reasons that others can examine and answer.

en.title: Logic and the Analysis of Argument
en.short: Statements, arguments, validity and soundness, deduction and induction, fallacies, and truth tables.

sections.heading: Statements and arguments
sections.text: A statement, or proposition, is a declarative sentence that is true or false. “The library opens at eight” is a statement; a question is not. An argument is a set of statements where some, the premises, give reasons for another, the conclusion. The premises are claimed to support the conclusion; the conclusion is what the arguer wants accepted. A mere explanation may not be an argument; look for the inferential claim.

sections.heading: Validity and soundness
sections.text: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all premises to be true and the conclusion false. Validity concerns form, not whether premises are true. It is sound when valid and every premise is true, so a sound argument has a true conclusion. Example: All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. Therefore Socrates is mortal. This form is valid; with true premises it is sound. A valid argument with a false premise is unsound.

sections.heading: Deduction and induction
sections.text: Deduction aims at validity: the conclusion is meant to follow with necessity. Induction aims at support: the premises make the conclusion probable. “Every swan I have seen is white, so all swans are white” is inductive; it can be strong yet have a false conclusion. Deductive arguments are valid or invalid; inductive ones strong or weak. A cogent inductive argument is strong and has true premises. Adding cases does not turn induction into deduction.

sections.heading: Fallacies and symbols
sections.text: A formal fallacy is an error in logical form, such as affirming the consequent: If P then Q; Q; therefore P. Informal fallacies include ad hominem (attacking the person), straw man (misrepresenting an opponent), false dilemma (only two options), begging the question (assuming the conclusion) and hasty generalisation (too few cases). Capital letters stand for statements. Symbols: ¬ not, ∧ and, ∨ or, → if then, ↔ if and only if. For P → Q, a truth table gives: T T gives T; T F gives F; F T gives T; F F gives T. The conditional is false only when P is true and Q false.

keyPoints: A statement is true or false; an argument uses premises to support a conclusion.
Validity is about form: no possible case where premises are true and conclusion false.
Soundness requires validity plus true premises.
Deduction aims at necessity; induction at probability, assessed as strong or weak.
Formal fallacies break logical form; informal fallacies depend on content or context.
In propositional notation ¬, ∧, ∨, → and ↔ mean not, and, or, if then, and if and only if.

en.title: Critical Thinking and Reasoning Skills
en.short: Charitable reconstruction, hidden premises, judging evidence and sources, and inductive strength.

sections.heading: Charitable reconstruction
sections.text: To reconstruct an argument is to set out its premises (the reasons offered) and its conclusion (the claim they support) in your own words, in the strongest form the writer could accept. The principle of charity says: read an unclear passage in the most reasonable way it allows, and say what you changed. A steel-man is stronger than the original; a straw man is weaker. Charity is not agreement: you may still reject the conclusion.

sections.heading: Finding hidden premises
sections.text: Most real arguments leave premises unstated; an argument with a missing premise is an enthymeme. To find the gap, ask what must be true for the stated reasons to support the conclusion. Example: 'Kofi is a medical student, so he will do well in statistics.' The hidden assumption is that medical students generally do well in statistics. Then ask whether it is true.

sections.heading: Evidence and sources
sections.text: Ask of any source: who wrote it, what they know, when, and for whom. A primary source is the original document, data set or report; a secondary source describes it. Peer review, checking by other experts before publication, lowers error but does not remove it. Watch for small or self-selected samples. A campus paper reports that '9 out of 10 students prefer the new timetable'. If only 10 were asked, 9 ÷ 10 = 90%, but that cannot support a claim about a university of thousands. Correlation does not by itself show causation.

sections.heading: Reasoning under uncertainty
sections.text: Inductive reasoning generalises from observed cases to unobserved ones. It is strong when the sample is large and representative and the conclusion modest; weak when the sample is small or biased, or the conclusion sweeping. 'Three buses left late, so all do' is weak. 'In a random sample of 400 of 5,000 students, 320 used the library, so about 80% do' is stronger: 320 ÷ 400 = 80%. To test a claim, state it precisely, list evidence for and against, check the source, and give your confidence, not a bare yes or no.

keyPoints: Reconstruct an argument charitably: state its premises and conclusion in the strongest form the writer would accept, and say what you changed.
An enthymeme is an argument with an unstated premise; find it by asking what must be true for the reasons to support the conclusion.
Check sources for authorship, expertise, date and purpose; peer review reduces error but does not guarantee truth.
Small or self-selected samples support only weak generalisations, however striking the percentage looks.
Inductive strength rises with sample size, representativeness and a modest conclusion.
Correlation alone does not establish causation; look for a mechanism and for other factors that could explain both.

en.title: Methods of Philosophical Inquiry
en.short: Conceptual analysis, thought experiments, counterexamples, reflective equilibrium and defending a view.

sections.heading: Framing a problem
sections.text:
A philosophical problem is framed by making the question precise. Ask what kind of question it is: a question of fact (how many people?), of meaning (what does the word mean?) or of justification (is this right?). Define the key terms, then state a position as a claim with reasons.

Test the claim against objections, and state each objection in its strongest form. This is the principle of charity: answer the best version of the opposing view, not a weak one.

sections.heading: Conceptual analysis
sections.text:
Conceptual analysis asks for the conditions under which a term applies. A necessary condition must be present for the term to apply; a sufficient condition is enough on its own. A definition usually offers conditions that are both.

Test it with a counterexample: a case where the definition and a confident judgement disagree. Suppose art is defined as whatever is displayed in a gallery. A fire extinguisher on a gallery wall is displayed there, but it is not art, so the definition fails as it stands. Narrow it or drop it.

sections.heading: Thought experiments
sections.text:
A thought experiment describes an imagined case, stripped of distractions, so that one principle can be tested. It works only if the case is described clearly and your judgement about it is firm.

Reflective equilibrium, a term associated with John Rawls, means moving back and forth between particular judgements and general principles, revising each until they agree. If a principle condemns a case you are sure is right, either the principle or the judgement has to change.

sections.heading: Description and history
sections.text:
Phenomenological description reports experience as it appears, setting aside the question of whether it is real. Edmund Husserl called this bracketing (epoché). It maps concepts such as attention or grief before they are explained.

History of ideas studies how a problem and its vocabulary arose. It guards against anachronism: reading later meanings back into older texts.

keyPoints: A position is a claim with reasons, defended against the strongest objection you can find.
Conceptual analysis states necessary and sufficient conditions for a term.
One clear counterexample can defeat a definition as stated.
A thought experiment isolates a principle by describing an imagined case.
Reflective equilibrium adjusts judgements and principles until they cohere.
Phenomenological description reports experience before explaining it, and history of ideas guards against anachronism.

en.title: Early Greek Philosophy: Presocratics, Socrates and Plato
en.short: Presocratic inquiry, the Socratic method, Plato’s Forms, knowledge, soul and justice in the Republic.

sections.heading: From myth to reason
sections.text: The Presocratics were thinkers before Socrates who sought natural explanations rather than stories about gods. Thales of Miletus said all things come from water, a claim about a basic substance. Heraclitus stressed constant change and a rational order (logos) in the world. Parmenides argued that change is an illusion because what is cannot become what is not. Democritus held that reality consists of atoms and empty space. These are early reasoned proposals, not experiments; they show the move from myth to inquiry.

sections.heading: Socrates and method
sections.text: Socrates wrote nothing; Plato presents him in dialogues. The Socratic method is question and answer that exposes inconsistency. In a typical case, Socrates asks what courage is. A general answers that courage is standing firm in battle. Socrates notes that a soldier who retreats wisely may still be brave, so the definition is too narrow. The aim is not to win but to test beliefs and seek a general definition. Socrates called himself ignorant and questioned experts.

sections.heading: Forms and knowledge
sections.text: Plato argued that sensible things are imperfect copies of eternal Forms, which are abstract patterns such as Beauty itself. Knowledge, for Plato, is of Forms; opinion concerns changing things. In the allegory of the cave, prisoners mistake shadows for reality until they turn toward the light. The soul is immortal and learns by recollection, though the details vary across dialogues. The body can distract it, but reason can guide it toward truth.

sections.heading: Justice in the Republic
sections.text: In the Republic, Plato asks whether justice is good in itself or only for its rewards. He describes a just soul as one where reason rules, spirit supports it, and appetite obeys. A just city mirrors this: rulers, soldiers and producers each do their own work. Socrates answers Glaucon’s challenge by arguing that the just life is happier and more unified. Critics ask whether his ideal city is too authoritarian, and whether the analogy between soul and city holds.

keyPoints: The Presocratics replaced myth with reasoned accounts of nature.
Thales proposed water as a basic substance, Heraclitus stressed change and logos, Parmenides denied change, and Democritus taught atoms.
The Socratic method uses questions to expose inconsistency and seek general definitions.
Plato’s Forms are eternal patterns; knowledge is of Forms, while opinion concerns changing things.
Plato describes the soul as immortal and tripartite, with reason meant to rule.
In the Republic justice is harmony in the soul and city, each part doing its own work.

en.title: Aristotle and the Hellenistic Schools
en.short: Aristotle on substance, causes, knowledge and virtue; Epicurean, Stoic and Sceptic answers.

sections.heading: Aristotle on substance
sections.text: Aristotle asks what really exists. Primary substance is the individual thing, such as this person or this tree. Form is the essence that makes it the kind of thing it is; matter is what it is made of. A bronze sphere, for example, has bronze as matter and spherical shape as form. Aristotle explains change with four causes: the material cause (what it is made of), the formal cause (its structure or essence), the efficient cause (what brought it about) and the final cause (its purpose or end). His epistemology is broadly empiricist: knowledge begins with sense perception, memory builds experience, and experience supports general principles, though reason grasps them.

sections.heading: Virtue and the mean
sections.text: Virtue ethics asks what kind of person to be. For Aristotle, eudaimonia (flourishing or happiness) is the goal, and virtues are stable dispositions to act and feel well. Each virtue is a mean between two vices: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. The mean is not a fixed average; it is the right response, in the right amount, at the right time, guided by practical wisdom (phronesis). A soldier who runs from every danger is cowardly; one who charges needlessly is reckless; the courageous person judges the situation. Virtue is learned through habit and good upbringing.

sections.heading: Hellenistic rivals
sections.text: After Aristotle, three schools offered rival answers about happiness, nature and knowledge. Epicureans hold that pleasure is the highest good, but by pleasure they mean freedom from bodily pain and tranquillity of mind (ataraxia). They favour simple pleasures, friendship and withdrawal from politics; their physics is atomistic. Stoics hold that virtue alone is good and that we should live according to nature, meaning rational order. We control our judgements, not external events, so the wise person is calm. Sceptics argue that for many questions equally strong arguments support both sides. They suspend judgement (epoché) to reach tranquillity, and so question whether firm knowledge is available. These schools disagree about what happiness is and how far knowledge can go.

keyPoints: For Aristotle, primary substance is the individual thing, and form is its essence.
Aristotle’s four causes are material, formal, efficient and final.
Aristotle holds that knowledge begins with sense experience and is guided by reason.
Virtue for Aristotle is a mean between excess and deficiency, chosen by practical wisdom.
Epicureans seek freedom from pain and disturbance through simple pleasures and friendship.
Stoics seek virtue and calm by living according to nature and controlling judgement; Sceptics suspend judgement to reach tranquillity.

en.title: Medieval, Islamic and Early African Philosophy
en.short: Augustine, Boethius and Aquinas on faith, reason and universals, then Islamic and early African philosophy.

sections.heading: Faith and reason
sections.text:
Augustine (354-430), bishop of Hippo in North Africa, held that faith and reason work together: believe first, then seek understanding. Reason clarifies what faith holds, but it does not replace it.

Boethius (c. 477-524), a Roman, wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison and passed the problem of universals to the Middle Ages. Aquinas (1225-1274) argued that reason can prove some truths about God, such as his existence, but others, such as the Trinity, come only by revelation.

sections.heading: Universals and God-talk
sections.text:
Universals are properties shared by many things, such as redness. Realists say they exist independently; moderate realists, like Aquinas, say they exist in things but are grasped by the mind; nominalists such as Ockham say they are only names.

On divine attributes Aquinas holds that we cannot say what God is, only what God is not, so words like good apply by analogy, not in the same sense as for creatures.

sections.heading: Islamic philosophers
sections.text:
Al-Kindi, in ninth-century Baghdad, argued that philosophy and revelation teach one truth. Al-Farabi pictured a virtuous city ruled by a philosopher-prophet, with religion as a symbolic image of philosophical truth.

Ibn Sina (Avicenna) used the Floating Man case: a person suspended in air, cut off from all sensation, still knows that he exists, so the soul knows itself without the senses. He also argued from contingency to a necessary being. Ibn Rushd (Averroes) of Cordoba answered al-Ghazali’s attack on philosophy in The Incoherence of the Incoherence.

sections.heading: African philosophy
sections.text:
Ethnophilosophy presents a people’s shared worldview, proverbs and myths as philosophy, as Tempels did for the Bantu. Hountondji rejected it: philosophy must be individual, critical and written, not unanimous.

Odera Oruka’s sage philosophy recorded the reasoned views of Kenyan elders, showing critical thought inside tradition. Professional philosophy is the work of trained academics such as Wiredu and Bodunrin. Suppose a student writes that the elders say the world is a living whole. Hountondji asks who makes the claim and whether it can be criticised; Oruka asks whether an elder can defend it with reasons.

keyPoints: Augustine held that faith comes first and understanding follows; Aquinas held that reason proves some truths about God but not all.
Boethius passed Porphyry’s questions about universals to the medieval West, where realists, moderate realists and nominalists disagreed.
Aquinas says we know God by negation and analogy, not by direct description.
Al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd both held that religion and philosophy teach one truth at different levels.
Ibn Sina argued from the contingency of things to a necessary being, and used the Floating Man to show self-knowledge without the senses.
The African philosophy debate asks whether collective worldviews, the reasoning of sages, or academic work counts as philosophy.

en.title: Rationalism and Empiricism
en.short: Rationalists and empiricists on innate ideas, substance, experience, causation and Hume’s scepticism.

sections.heading: The dispute
sections.text:
Rationalism holds that reason is the chief source of knowledge and can reach truths experience cannot give. Empiricism holds that all knowledge comes from sense experience.

Both sides ask about ideas in the mind, but disagree about their origin and justification. The debate shaped seventeenth and eighteenth century philosophy in Europe.

sections.heading: Rationalists
sections.text:
Descartes argued that some ideas, such as the idea of God and of perfect geometrical truths, are innate: inborn capacities or dispositions rather than copies of experience. He defined substance as something that exists independently. He held that mind and body are two created substances, a view called dualism.

Spinoza denied two substances: he argued that only one substance, God or Nature, exists, and thought and extension are its attributes. Leibniz held that reality consists of monads, simple immaterial substances, each mirroring the universe. For rationalists, reason can uncover necessary truths about substance.

sections.heading: Empiricists
sections.text:
Locke rejected innate ideas. He compared the mind to a blank tablet, a tabula rasa, and argued that all ideas come from sensation and reflection. Simple ideas combine into complex ones.

Berkeley accepted experience but denied material substance: we know only ideas and the minds that have them; for ideas, to be is to be perceived. Hume divided perceptions into impressions, which are vivid, and ideas, which are faint copies. He argued that causation is not observed as a necessary power. We see one event follow another, a constant conjunction, and form a habit of expectation.

sections.heading: Hume’s scepticism
sections.text:
Suppose a billiard ball strikes another. We observe motion and contact, not a visible power making the second ball move. Hume concludes that we infer causation from constant conjunction, not from reason.

Induction, reasoning from past cases to future ones, has the same weakness: past sunrises do not prove tomorrow’s. On the self, introspection finds only particular perceptions, never a permanent owner. The self is a bundle of perceptions. These problems still frame debates about knowledge.

keyPoints: Rationalism treats reason as the main route to knowledge; empiricism treats sense experience as its source.
Descartes held innate ideas and dualism; Spinoza one substance; Leibniz monads.
Locke denied innate ideas and compared the mind to a blank tablet.
Berkeley denied material substance; Hume reduced causation to constant conjunction and habit.
Hume’s induction problem says past regularities cannot prove future ones.
Hume’s bundle theory says the self is only a collection of perceptions.

en.title: Kant and the Idealist Response
en.short: Kant’s critical philosophy, the Copernican turn, limits of reason, and Hegel’s absolute idealism.

sections.heading: Kant’s distinction
sections.text: Immanuel Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason (1781, revised 1787) asks what the mind contributes to experience. An analytic judgement is true by meaning: 'all bachelors are unmarried' adds no new information. A synthetic judgement adds information: 'this stone is heavy'. Kant also claimed synthetic a priori judgements, known independently of experience yet informative. He held that arithmetic, such as 7 + 5 = 12, is an example. The distinction separates knowledge by definition from knowledge through experience.

sections.heading: Copernican turn
sections.text: Kant’s Copernican turn reverses the usual picture. Instead of assuming our concepts must fit objects, he argues that objects of experience must fit the conditions of our cognition. Space and time are forms of intuition: the mind’s a priori ways of arranging sensory input. The categories are pure concepts of the understanding, such as substance and causality, which make experience possible. We therefore know appearances, not things in themselves. For example, we experience events as caused because causality is a condition of unified experience.

sections.heading: Limits of reason
sections.text: Theoretical reason seeks knowledge of what is. Kant argues it overreaches when it tries to prove claims beyond possible experience. The antinomies are pairs of contradictory conclusions that reason reaches about the world, such as whether the world has a beginning in time. Kant resolves them by distinguishing appearances from things in themselves. This limits theoretical reason: God, freedom and immortality are not objects of theoretical knowledge. They belong to practical reason, or moral faith.

sections.heading: Hegel’s idealism
sections.text: German idealists reacted to Kant’s dualism. Fichte and Schelling tried to overcome the thing in itself, but Hegel is central. In absolute idealism, reality is a rational whole, spirit or Geist, developing in history. Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) traces how consciousness comes to recognise that its own rational activity shapes the world it knows. His dialectic describes thought moving through contradiction and resolution, not a fixed formula. Absolute idealism rejects Kant’s unknowable thing in itself and treats the rational structure of thought as the structure of reality.

keyPoints: Kant’s analytic judgements are true by meaning, while synthetic judgements add information.
Kant’s Copernican turn says objects of experience must conform to the conditions of our cognition.
Space and time are forms of intuition, and the categories are pure concepts that make experience possible.
The antinomies show theoretical reason overreaching beyond possible experience.
Hegel’s absolute idealism treats reality as a rational whole developing through history.
German idealism rejected Kant’s unknowable thing in itself.

en.title: Logic, Language and the Philosophy of Science
en.short: Predicate logic, Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, verification, Popper, Kuhn and Lakatos.

sections.heading: Predicate logic
sections.text: Modern predicate logic analyses arguments with predicates, variables and quantifiers. A predicate such as Hx says that x is human; ∀ means “for all” and ∃ means “there exists”. The argument “All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal” becomes ∀x(Hx→Mx), Hs, therefore Ms. The form is valid: no interpretation makes the premises true and the conclusion false.

sections.heading: Meaning and reference
sections.text: Gottlob Frege distinguished sense from reference. “The morning star” and “the evening star” refer to the same planet, Venus, but present it differently; that difference is sense. Bertrand Russell analysed definite descriptions, such as “the so-and-so”. He argued that “The present king of France is bald” is not a subject-predicate claim but a conjunction: there is one king of France, and he is bald. There is no such king, so the sentence is false. Ludwig Wittgenstein, in the Tractatus (1921), held that propositions picture facts and are true when they agree with reality.

sections.heading: Verification and its critics
sections.text: The logical positivists of the Vienna Circle, including Moritz Schlick and Rudolf Carnap, proposed the verification principle: a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified by experience or is true by definition. They rejected metaphysical and theological claims as meaningless. Critics objected that the principle itself cannot be verified by experience. A. J. Ayer softened it to weak verifiability, but the difficulty remained. Meaning, critics said, is broader than verification.

sections.heading: Science and theory change
sections.text: Karl Popper proposed falsification: a scientific hypothesis must be testable and could be refuted by observation. One counterexample can falsify a universal law. Thomas Kuhn (1962) described normal science within a paradigm, a framework of assumptions and methods. Anomalies accumulate and may trigger a revolution; the new paradigm is not chosen by logic alone, and Kuhn spoke of incommensurability. Imre Lakatos offered research programmes with a hard core of protected assumptions and a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses. A programme is progressive if it predicts new facts, degenerating if it only patches problems.

keyPoints: Predicate logic uses quantifiers to show why an argument such as ∀x(Hx→Mx), Hs, therefore Ms is valid.
Frege separated sense from reference, Russell analysed definite descriptions, and early Wittgenstein held that propositions picture facts.
The logical positivists’ verification principle held that meaningful statements are verifiable by experience or true by definition.
Critics said the verification principle fails its own test and that meaning is broader than verification.
Popper proposed falsification, Kuhn described paradigms and revolutions, and Lakatos described research programmes with a hard core and protective belt.
Scientific change involves both evidence and framework assumptions, so no single method fully captures it.

en.title: Phenomenology and Existentialism
en.short: Covers Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, Beauvoir, anxiety, authenticity and Camus’s absurd.

sections.heading: Husserl’s phenomenology
sections.text: Edmund Husserl (1859-1938) wanted philosophy to describe experience as it appears, not explain it by causes. His phenomenological reduction brackets, or sets aside, assumptions about whether things exist, then describes what is given to consciousness. He called this epoché. Intentionality is the claim that consciousness is always consciousness of something. Experience has an act of awareness, noesis, and an object as meant, noema. Perceiving a cup is already a seeing-as, shaped by meaning.

sections.heading: Heidegger’s Being
sections.text: Martin Heidegger (1889-1976) asked the question of Being: what does it mean for anything to be? In Being and Time (1927) he analyses Dasein, the kind of being we are. Dasein is being-in-the-world: not a mind inside a body but always engaged with tools, projects and other people. Things show up as ready-to-hand when we use them, and as present-at-hand when we inspect them. Anxiety reveals our own possibilities, including death.

sections.heading: Sartre and Beauvoir
sections.text: Jean-Paul Sartre (1905-1980) held that consciousness is intentional and has no fixed content. Existence precedes essence: we first exist, then make ourselves through choices. Freedom is radical and brings anguish. Bad faith is self-deception in which we deny our freedom, for example by saying “I had no choice” or treating ourselves as a fixed role. Simone de Beauvoir applied this to gender. In The Second Sex (1949) she argued that woman is defined as the Other in relation to man, and that one becomes a woman through social conditioning.

sections.heading: Anxiety, absurd, authenticity
sections.text: Existentialism is a family of themes. Anxiety is unease at freedom and uncertainty, not fear of a specific object. Authenticity means owning one’s choices rather than living by convention or bad faith. Albert Camus (1913-1960) called the absurd the clash between our demand for meaning and the world’s silence. In The Myth of Sisyphus he answers with revolt, not suicide. A student in Nairobi whose family prefers one course can choose it honestly, or tell herself she “must” obey; Sartre would call the second bad faith.

keyPoints: Husserl’s phenomenological reduction brackets existence claims to describe experience; intentionality means consciousness is always of something.
Heidegger asks the question of Being and analyses Dasein as being-in-the-world.
Sartre holds that existence precedes essence, that freedom brings anguish, and that bad faith denies freedom.
Beauvoir argues that woman is made the Other and that one becomes a woman through social conditioning.
Anxiety, authenticity and the absurd are existential themes, but existentialists disagree on doctrine.
Camus treats the absurd as the clash between the demand for meaning and the world’s silence, and answers with revolt.

en.title: Analytic Philosophy: Mind, Meaning and Ordinary Language
en.short: Russell, the Vienna Circle, Wittgenstein, Austin and Ryle, and the analytic style.

sections.heading: Russell and analysis
sections.text:
Bertrand Russell’s theory of descriptions (1905) treats “the present King of France” not as a name but as a quantified description. “The F is G” means: there is an F; there is at most one F; and whatever is F is G.

So “The present King of France is bald” is false, not meaningless: it asserts that a unique king exists, which is false. Breaking sentences into logical form became central to analytic argument.

sections.heading: Vienna Circle
sections.text:
The Vienna Circle, a Vienna group of the 1920s and 1930s, included Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap and Otto Neurath. Logical positivism held that a statement is meaningful only if it is analytic, true by meaning, or empirically verifiable. Metaphysical sentences were called meaningless.

The verification principle was soon criticised: general laws cannot be conclusively verified, and the principle itself is neither analytic nor verifiable. Verificationism was largely abandoned, but its demand for clarity and testable claims influenced analytic philosophy.

sections.heading: Wittgenstein on games
sections.text:
The later Wittgenstein, especially in Philosophical Investigations (1953), rejected the idea that every word has one fixed meaning. Meaning is use within a language game, a rule-governed activity such as giving orders, counting or telling a joke. Words can share family resemblances without a single essence.

He also asks what makes following a rule correct. No private formula fixes every future application; shared training and custom, a form of life, guide us. Rules gain authority from practice.

sections.heading: Ordinary language and mind
sections.text:
J. L. Austin examined ordinary language closely and developed speech act theory. A performative utterance such as “I promise” does something rather than merely describe.

Gilbert Ryle, in The Concept of Mind (1949), attacked Cartesian dualism as a category mistake: mind and body are not two items of the same kind. Talk of beliefs and wants describes dispositions to behave, not a ghost in a machine. These thinkers made analytic philosophy attentive to use, example and counterexample.

keyPoints: Russell analysed definite descriptions as quantified claims about existence and uniqueness, not as names.
The Vienna Circle’s verification principle made empirical testability the mark of meaning, but it was largely abandoned after criticism.
Wittgenstein’s later work treats meaning as use in rule-governed language games and grounds rule-following in shared practice.
Austin’s speech act theory shows that some utterances perform actions rather than describe facts.
Ryle called Cartesian dualism a category mistake and analysed mental terms as dispositions to behave.
Analytic philosophy’s style is clarity, logical analysis, small distinctions, examples and counterexamples.

en.title: African Philosophy: Debates and Key Thinkers
en.short: The four positions, personhood and Ubuntu, and key thinkers from Hountondji to Menkiti.

sections.heading: Four positions
sections.text: The debate asks whether African philosophy exists and what form it takes. Ethnophilosophy treats the collective worldviews, proverbs, myths and religious beliefs of African peoples as philosophy. Sage philosophy, developed by Henry Odera Oruka, records traditional thinkers and separates folk sagacity, wise sayings, from philosophic sagacity, critical reflection on one’s culture. Professional philosophy is practised by trained academics who use critical argument and written texts; Paulin Hountondji and Kwasi Wiredu are leading examples. Nationalist-ideological philosophy is the political thought of independence leaders and ideologues, such as Kwame Nkrumah’s consciencism, Julius Nyerere’s Ujamaa and Leopold Senghor’s Negritude. It seeks identity and development, but critics say it can become propaganda.

sections.heading: Critique and method
sections.text: Hountondji attacked ethnophilosophy as unanimous and uncritical, insisting philosophy is individual critical discourse. Wiredu proposes conceptual decolonisation: examine inherited concepts and keep what survives argument. Gyekye defends a moderate communitarianism, while Menkiti holds that community is prior to the individual and personhood is earned through moral maturity.

sections.heading: Personhood and Ubuntu
sections.text: The communitarian debate concerns personhood. Menkiti argues that a person becomes a person through community and moral achievement; Gyekye replies that community and individual are complementary, and individual rights and dignity remain. Ubuntu, a Southern African idea, is often rendered 'a person is a person through other persons'. It stresses relational humanity and mutual care, but scholars warn that it is not a single doctrine and can hide individuality, gender inequality and conflict.

sections.heading: Case
sections.text: Case: a student quotes an Akan proverb as proof of African philosophy. Hountondji would ask for critical argument, Oruka might seek a sage’s reasoned defence, and Gyekye would place the proverb in a shared but debated tradition. The point is not to reject tradition but to test it.

keyPoints: Ethnophilosophy treats collective African worldviews as philosophy, while Oruka’s sage philosophy separates wise sayings from critical reflection.
Professional philosophy insists on critical, written argument, and Hountondji attacked ethnophilosophy as uncritical and unanimous.
Nationalist-ideological philosophy uses ideas such as consciencism, Ujamaa and Negritude for identity and development.
Menkiti holds that community is prior and personhood is earned; Gyekye defends a moderate communitarianism of individual and community.
Ubuntu stresses relational personhood and mutual care but is not a single doctrine.
Wiredu’s conceptual decolonisation asks thinkers to test inherited concepts by argument.

en.title: Metaphysics: Reality, Substance and Causation
en.short: Universals, substance, abstract objects, causation, space, time and change, with realist and nominalist replies.

sections.heading: Universals and particulars
sections.text: Metaphysics asks what exists. A particular is a single thing, such as this mango. A universal is a shared property or kind, such as redness. Realists say universals exist independently: Plato placed Forms apart from things; Aristotle held forms in things. Nominalists deny independent universals; only particulars exist, and general words name resemblances or serve our purposes. Realists argue that many red things share one property, which needs explanation. Nominalists reply that universals add entities with no causal work.

sections.heading: Substance and property
sections.text: Substance is what bears properties and persists through change; a property is a feature of it. Bundle theories identify a thing with its properties. Substratum theories posit a bare bearer beneath them. Abstract objects, such as numbers and propositions, are defined as non-spatial and non-causal. Platonists say they exist independently; nominalists and fictionalists deny this or treat them as useful fictions. The number 7 cannot be seen or touched, yet arithmetic seems true. The dispute is whether truth requires an object.

sections.heading: Causation and powers
sections.text: Causation concerns how one event produces another. Regularity theories say causation is constant conjunction: one kind of event follows another, and we form an expectation. Counterfactual theories say a cause makes a difference: without it, the effect would not occur. Powers theories say things have dispositions, real tendencies to act. A match lights when struck because it is flammable in oxygen, not merely because striking and lighting often occur together. Regularists avoid mysterious necessary connections; powers theorists say those connections explain the pattern.

sections.heading: Space, time and change
sections.text: Space and time are either substantival, existing as entities in their own right, or relational, being orders among things and events. The problem of change asks how one thing can gain and lose properties. Endurantists say the whole leaf persists while its colour changes. Perdurantists say it has temporal parts, so green and brown belong to different parts. Each view must explain identity through time without making change illusory or replacing one thing by another.

keyPoints: Particulars are individual things; universals are shared properties or kinds.
Realists hold that universals exist independently; nominalists deny this and explain generality by resemblance, names or use.
Substance bears properties and persists; bundle and substratum theories disagree about what that bearer is.
Abstract objects are non-spatial and non-causal; Platonists accept them, nominalists and fictionalists reject or reinterpret them.
Regularity theories treat causation as constant conjunction; powers theories posit real dispositions.
Space and time may be substantival or relational, and endurantism and perdurantism offer different answers to change.

en.title: Free Will, Determinism and Personal Identity
en.short: Free will positions, the consequence and luck arguments, and personal identity through memory and continuity.

sections.heading: Free will positions
sections.text: Determinism says every event, including each choice, is fixed by earlier causes and laws. Libertarianism says some choices are free in a sense requiring the ability to have done otherwise, and determinism is false. Compatibilism says freedom and responsibility fit determinism: a free act flows from the agent’s own desires and reasoning, not external force. Critics ask whether this gives the control responsibility needs.

sections.heading: Consequence and luck
sections.text: The consequence argument says that if determinism is true, our acts follow from the past and laws we did not choose, so we cannot do otherwise. Libertarians reply that agents can originate actions, though critics call this mysterious. The luck argument says an uncaused free choice seems random, not the agent’s; a fully caused one seems determined. This dilemma presses libertarianism. Compatibilists say responsibility needs action to flow from settled character, not to be uncaused.

sections.heading: Personal identity
sections.text: Locke held that identity over time consists in continuity of consciousness, especially memory: you are the same person as a past self if you can remember that self’s experiences. Psychological continuity theories broaden this to overlapping memories, beliefs, intentions and character. Bodily criteria say identity depends on the same living body or brain. If Amina wakes after an accident with her memories and plans intact but a changed body, psychological views call her the same person; a pure bodily view may disagree.

sections.heading: Reductionism
sections.text: Reductionist views, associated with Derek Parfit, deny that personal identity is a further fact beyond physical and psychological continuity. What matters in survival is continuity of mental life, not whether an identical self persists. If a person’s psychology divides between two bodies, we ask what matters rather than which one is really her. Critics say reductionism cannot explain the unity of experience or our concern for the future.

keyPoints: Determinism holds that every event, including choices, is fixed by earlier causes and laws.
Libertarianism denies determinism and claims free choices require the ability to do otherwise.
Compatibilism treats freedom as acting from one’s own desires and reasoning, even under determinism.
The consequence argument says determinism removes alternative possibilities; the luck argument says uncaused choices seem random.
Locke’s memory criterion and psychological continuity theories locate personal identity in continuity of consciousness.
Reductionism, associated with Parfit, says what matters is psychological continuity, not a further identical self.

en.title: Philosophy of Mind
en.short: Dualism, behaviourism, identity theory, functionalism, qualia, mental causation and the extended mind.

sections.heading: Five positions
sections.text:
Substance dualism, associated with Descartes, holds that mind and body are distinct substances. It faces the interaction problem: how can a nonphysical mind affect a physical body? Philosophical behaviourism, linked to Ryle, treats mental terms as dispositions to behave, but it struggles with inner experience.

The identity theory says mental states are brain states, not merely correlated with them. Functionalism defines a mental state by its causal role between inputs, other states and outputs, so it could be realised in brains or machines. Property dualism accepts one physical substance but holds that mental properties, such as pain, are irreducible.

sections.heading: Qualia and consciousness
sections.text:
Qualia are the subjective, felt qualities of experience, such as the redness of red. The knowledge argument imagines Mary, who knows every physical fact about colour but has never seen it. On seeing red, she seems to learn something new; Frank Jackson argues this shows physical facts do not exhaust reality.

The zombie argument asks whether a being physically identical to you but with no inner experience is conceivable. David Chalmers argues that if it is conceivable, it may be possible, so consciousness is not merely physical. Critics reply that conceivability does not prove possibility.

sections.heading: Mental causation
sections.text:
Mental causation is the claim that thoughts cause physical events. If mental properties are nonphysical, it is hard to explain how they make a difference.

Epiphenomenalism says mental events are byproducts with no causal power. Identity theory and functionalism find causation easier because mental states are physical or realised physically.

sections.heading: Extended mind and AI
sections.text:
The extended mind thesis of Clark and Chalmers says some cognitive processes include external objects. In their case, Otto with memory loss uses a notebook as reliable memory, so the notebook is part of his cognitive system. Critics dispute the boundary.

Cognitive science and artificial intelligence support functionalism by modelling mental processes as computation. John Searle’s Chinese room argues that symbol manipulation alone gives syntax, not understanding or consciousness.

keyPoints: Substance dualism holds that mind and body are distinct substances, but it faces the interaction problem.
Behaviourism reduces mental talk to behavioural dispositions, while identity theory identifies mental states with brain states.
Functionalism defines mental states by causal role and allows multiple realisation; property dualism treats mental properties as irreducible.
Qualia are subjective felt qualities, and the knowledge and zombie arguments use them to challenge physicalism.
Mental causation asks how nonphysical mental properties can affect physical events; epiphenomenalism denies such power.
The extended mind thesis and AI debates ask whether cognition can include external objects or computation alone.

en.title: Epistemology: Knowledge and Justification
en.short: JTB, Gettier cases, foundationalism, coherentism, reliabilism, scepticism and contextualism.

sections.heading: Knowledge as JTB
sections.text: The traditional analysis says knowledge is justified true belief (JTB). You must believe the claim, it must be true, and you must have justification for it. Each condition seems necessary, but Edmund Gettier’s 1963 paper showed they are not jointly sufficient. In a typical case, Smith has strong evidence for a false claim P and justifiably infers Q from P. Q happens to be true by luck. Smith has a justified true belief in Q, yet most philosophers say he does not know it. The case is a counterexample to the JTB analysis.

sections.heading: Justification theories
sections.text: Foundationalism holds that some basic beliefs are justified without inference, and other beliefs rest on them. Coherentism denies foundations: a belief is justified by fitting into a coherent system of beliefs that support one another. Reliabilism says a belief is justified when produced by a reliable process, such as perception or sound reasoning, whether or not the believer can show why.

sections.heading: Internalism and externalism
sections.text: Internalism says justifying factors must be accessible to the believer on reflection. Externalism says they need not be; reliability may be external to the mind. Reliabilism is usually externalist. The dispute asks what kind of thing justification is: a matter of the subject’s perspective or of how beliefs are formed.

sections.heading: Scepticism and context
sections.text: Dreaming and deception arguments ask how you can rule out that you are dreaming or being deceived. If you cannot, can you know anything? Contextualism replies that the standard for “knows” shifts with context. In ordinary talk, “I know there is a chair” may be true; in a philosophical discussion that raises sceptical possibilities, the standard rises and the same sentence may be false. This explains sceptical pressure without surrendering ordinary knowledge.

keyPoints: The traditional analysis defines knowledge as justified true belief.
Gettier cases show that justified true belief can fail to be knowledge.
Foundationalism grounds justification in basic beliefs; coherentism grounds it in mutual support.
Reliabilism justifies beliefs by the reliability of the processes that form them.
Internalism requires accessible justifying factors; externalism does not.
Contextualism says the standard for knowledge varies with context, which answers scepticism.

en.title: Ethics: Normative and Metaethical Theories
en.short: Normative theories of right action and metaethical debates on moral truth and value.

sections.heading: Normative theories
sections.text:
Normative ethics asks what makes an action right. Consequentialism judges acts by outcomes. Its classic form, utilitarianism, holds that the right act produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number; Bentham and Mill are key figures. Critics say it can permit injustice, ignore intentions and demand too much.

Deontology judges acts by duty and rules. Kant’s categorical imperative says act only on a maxim (a rule of action) you could will as universal law, and treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. Critics cite conflicting duties and indifference to consequences.

Virtue ethics asks what kind of person to be. Aristotle grounds it in eudaimonia, human flourishing, and in virtues such as courage, developed by habit and guided by phronesis, practical wisdom. Critics call it vague and not action-guiding; defenders say it explains character and moral education.

sections.heading: Metaethical questions
sections.text:
Metaethics asks whether moral claims can be true. Moral realism says moral facts exist independently of our beliefs, so “torture is wrong” is true or false. Emotivism (A. J. Ayer, C. L. Stevenson) says moral statements express feelings or attitudes and are not truth-apt, meaning not capable of truth or falsity.

Prescriptivism (R. M. Hare) says moral judgements are universal prescriptions: they guide action and commit us to judging similar cases alike. Error theory (J. L. Mackie) says moral claims are truth-apt but all false, because no objective moral properties exist; his “argument from queerness” says such properties would be unlike anything in nature.

sections.heading: Fact and value
sections.text:
The fact-value distinction separates descriptive claims about what is from evaluative claims about what ought to be. Hume’s is-ought gap says no ought conclusion follows from premises containing only is statements. Moore’s naturalistic fallacy warns against defining good by natural properties.

Case: a manager finds a worker is slower than others (fact). Whether to dismiss her depends on values such as fairness, not the fact alone.

keyPoints: Consequentialism judges right action by outcomes, especially the greatest happiness.
Kantian deontology judges action by universalisable maxims and respect for persons.
Virtue ethics centres on character, eudaimonia and practical wisdom.
Moral realism holds that moral facts exist independently of our attitudes.
Emotivism and prescriptivism treat moral language as expression or prescription, while error theory calls moral claims false.
Hume’s is-ought gap and Moore’s naturalistic fallacy warn against deriving values from facts alone.

en.title: Applied and Professional Ethics
en.short: How to analyse bioethics, business, professional and AI cases by weighing principles and facts.

sections.heading: Analysing a case
sections.text: Applied ethics starts with facts: stakeholders, options and uncertainties. Then apply moral theories and mid-level principles: respect for autonomy, beneficence (the duty to help), nonmaleficence (the duty not to harm) and justice. This approach is often called principlism, after Beauchamp and Childress. Ask what consequentialist, duty-based and virtue-based views say. Weigh the principles, explain conflicts, and justify the least harmful defensible choice. Laws and professional codes vary by country, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Bioethics
sections.text: Abortion and euthanasia are contested. Arguments turn on moral status, bodily autonomy, suffering and intention. Law differs by country. Resource allocation uses triage and cost-effectiveness to compare need, benefit and fairness. A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) is one measure, but it is controversial. Research consent requires disclosure, understanding, voluntariness and competence, plus ethics review. Case: Amina, a Nigerian hospital manager, has one ventilator and two patients. She must state criteria, apply them consistently and record reasons.

sections.heading: Business and professions
sections.text: Business ethics asks how firms should treat workers, customers, owners and communities. Professional ethics adds role duties, such as a doctor’s duty of care. Conflicts of interest, bribery, safety and whistleblowing are issues. A code is a guide, not a substitute for judgement. Case: a supplier offers a procurement officer a trip. Accepting it creates a conflict of interest and may breach policy. The officer should decline, disclose and follow the rules.

sections.heading: Information and AI
sections.text: Information ethics covers privacy, accuracy, ownership and access. AI adds bias, opacity, responsibility and consent. A hiring tool trained on past data may repeat discrimination. Users should test for bias, explain decisions, keep human review and protect data. Data protection law varies by country. Case: a Lagos bank’s AI rejects more women applicants. The bank should audit the data, pause the tool, and give applicants a reason and human appeal. Weigh efficiency against fairness and accountability.

keyPoints: Applied ethics analyses facts, stakeholders, options and principles before judging a case.
Principlism weighs autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence and justice, and conflicts must be explained.
Abortion, euthanasia, resource allocation and research consent are contested and regulated differently by country.
Professional ethics adds role duties and codes, and conflicts of interest should be disclosed.
Information ethics and AI raise privacy, bias, transparency and accountability concerns.
A defensible decision states criteria, applies them consistently and records reasons.

en.title: Social and Political Philosophy
en.short: Legitimacy, social contract, Rawls and Nozick on justice, liberty, equality, multiculturalism and African communalism.

sections.heading: Contract and obligation
sections.text: Why obey the state? Social contract theories ground legitimacy in consent, real or hypothetical. Thomas Hobbes says people escape a violent state of nature by authorising a sovereign. John Locke holds that government protects natural rights and may be resisted when it fails. Jean-Jacques Rousseau locates legitimacy in the general will. Political obligation is conditional, not absolute. The contract can be a thought experiment, not a historical event.

sections.heading: Justice and distribution
sections.text: Rawls asks what principles people would choose behind a veil of ignorance. He defends equal basic liberties, fair equality of opportunity, and the difference principle: inequalities are just only if they benefit the worst off. Nozick replies with an entitlement theory: justice depends on how holdings were acquired and transferred, not on a pattern. He defends a minimal state; taxing earnings for redistribution, he argues, treats persons as means. Critics include communitarians such as Sandel, who say Rawls ignores community, and Sen and Nussbaum, who ask what people can actually do and be. A school tax: Rawlsians ask if it helps the worst off; Nozickians ask whether the state may take earnings that were justly acquired.

sections.heading: Liberty, equality, culture
sections.text: Isaiah Berlin distinguishes negative liberty, the absence of interference, from positive liberty, being one’s own master. Limits on liberty need justification: John Stuart Mill’s harm principle permits restriction only to prevent harm to others. Equality can be formal, equal treatment, or substantive, equal outcomes or capabilities. Multiculturalism, associated with Will Kymlicka and Charles Taylor, asks whether liberal states should protect minority cultures through group rights or recognition.

sections.heading: African communalism
sections.text: African political thought stresses communalism: persons are constituted partly by community and have duties to it. Kwame Gyekye defends a moderate communitarianism that also respects individual rights. Kwasi Wiredu explores consensus decision-making in Akan tradition, where deliberation seeks agreement rather than a simple majority. In a village meeting on a borehole, elders keep talking until dissent is addressed. Critics ask whether consensus can silence minorities; defenders reply that it builds shared responsibility.

keyPoints: Social contract theories justify political obligation by consent, real or hypothetical, and make obedience conditional.
Rawls’s difference principle permits inequality only when it benefits the worst off.
Nozick’s entitlement theory judges justice by acquisition and transfer, not by a pattern.
Berlin distinguishes negative liberty (no interference) from positive liberty (self-mastery).
Multiculturalism asks whether liberal states should protect minority cultures through group rights or recognition.
African communalism stresses duties to community, while consensus democracy seeks agreement rather than simple majority rule.

en.title: Philosophy of Religion: Arguments, Evil and Belief
en.short: Classical arguments for God, the problem of evil, divine attributes, religious language and faith and reason.

sections.heading: Arguments for God
sections.text: The ontological argument, from Anselm and later Descartes, reasons from the idea of a greatest conceivable being to its existence. Kant replied that existence is not a predicate that adds to a concept. The cosmological argument, as in Aquinas and Leibniz, argues from contingency or change to a necessary first cause. Critics ask why the series cannot stop at the universe. The teleological argument, or design argument, reasons from order to a designer. Hume attacked the analogy, and Darwin later gave a natural explanation for apparent design. The argument from religious experience moves from reported encounters to God. William James treated such experiences as evidence; critics note that they differ across religions.

sections.heading: Evil and Attributes
sections.text: The problem of evil says an all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good God would not permit evil. The logical form claims evil is incompatible with God; the evidential form says evil makes belief unlikely. Defences include free will, soul-making and contrast. None is universally accepted. Omnipotence cannot mean doing contradictions, such as making a stone too heavy to lift. Omniscience and human freedom seem to conflict. A concrete case: a child’s preventable illness challenges claims that suffering always serves a purpose.

sections.heading: Religious Language
sections.text: Religious language is hard because talk of God uses words drawn from finite things. Aquinas held that terms apply analogically, neither univocally nor equivocally. Logical positivists demanded verification, and falsificationists asked what would count against belief. Both challenges are now seen as too strict. Wittgensteinians treat religious language as a language game with its own grammar. Apophatic theology stresses that God exceeds language.

sections.heading: Faith and Reason
sections.text: Faith and reason take several positions. Natural theology holds that reason alone can establish or support belief in God. Fideism says faith stands independently or above reason. Reformed epistemology, associated with Alvin Plantinga, holds that belief in God can be properly basic, not based on argument. The main positions are theism, atheism and agnosticism, with agnosticism suspending judgement. Ask whether an argument is deductive, inductive or experiential, and whether its conclusion follows.

keyPoints: The ontological argument moves from the concept of God to existence, while Kant denies that existence is a predicate.
The cosmological and teleological arguments infer a cause or designer, but critics question the inference.
Religious experience is offered as evidence, though experiences vary and are disputed.
The problem of evil challenges omnipotence, omniscience and omnibenevolence together.
Divine attributes create puzzles, such as omnipotence and contradictions or omniscience and free will.
Religious language may be analogical or apophatic, and faith and reason range from natural theology to fideism.

en.title: Aesthetics and the Philosophy of Art
en.short: Theories of art, beauty and judgement, ontology, interpretation, forgery, censorship and value.

sections.heading: Theories of art
sections.text: Imitation theory says art copies or represents reality; Plato distrusted images, while Aristotle thought imitation could teach and move. Expression theory says art expresses feeling, as in Tolstoy or Collingwood. Formalism, linked to Clive Bell and Roger Fry, values significant form, the arrangement of line, colour and shape, above subject matter. The institutional theory, linked to George Dickie, holds that an artefact becomes art when the artworld confers that status. Morris Weitz, following Wittgenstein, argued that art is a family resemblance concept with no single essence.

sections.heading: Beauty and judgement
sections.text: An aesthetic judgement is a judgement about beauty, sublimity or artistic merit. Kant held that judgements of taste are disinterested: we enjoy the form, not possession or use. They are subjective, resting on feeling, yet claim universal agreement. Beauty is therefore neither a simple objective property nor mere private preference. Hume argued that taste can be educated and that true judges, critics of trained sensibility, set the standard. Critics note that judgements are shaped by culture and power.

sections.heading: Ontology of art
sections.text: Ontology asks what kind of thing an artwork is. A painting is usually a singular physical object. A novel or symphony is repeatable: the work is a type, and performances or copies are tokens. This raises questions about authenticity. A perfect forgery may look identical, yet we value the original for its history and achievement. Arthur Danto and Nelson Goodman asked when something is art, not merely what it is.

sections.heading: Interpretation and value
sections.text: Interpretation asks whether meaning comes from the artist’s intention, the work, the audience or context. The intentional fallacy warns against reducing meaning to what the artist meant. Censorship raises whether art should be limited for offence, harm or politics; defenders of free art stress autonomy, while critics stress responsibility. Art’s value may be aesthetic, emotional, cognitive or moral. A forged painting can be beautiful, but its false history affects its value.

keyPoints: Imitation, expression, form, institutional and family resemblance theories give different answers to what makes something art.
Kant held that judgements of taste are disinterested and subjective yet claim universal assent.
Ontology distinguishes singular works, such as paintings, from repeatable works, such as novels and symphonies.
A perfect forgery can share appearance with an original but lacks its history and achievement.
Interpretation debates concern the artist’s intention, the work, the audience and context.
Censorship and value questions ask whether art should be limited and whether its worth is aesthetic, emotional, cognitive or moral.

en.title: Philosophy of Science: Demarcation, Explanation and Evidence
en.short: Demarcation, explanation, realism, theory-laden observation, inductive risk and research ethics.

sections.heading: Demarcation
sections.text: Demarcation asks what separates science from non-science. Logical positivists demanded verifiability, but universal laws cannot be verified by finite evidence. Karl Popper proposed falsifiability: a scientific claim forbids some observable outcome. Astrology fails because it can explain anything. Critics reply that science includes fruitful but hard-to-falsify ideas, and that pseudoscience sometimes makes testable claims. Thomas Kuhn stressed normal science within paradigms, shared frameworks of assumptions and methods. No single criterion is agreed.

sections.heading: Explanation and theory
sections.text: Carl Hempel’s covering-law model says an event is explained when it is deduced from general laws plus initial conditions. Statistical explanations use probability instead. Critics note that laws alone may not show the mechanism, so causal and mechanistic accounts ask how a cause produces an effect. Theories are organised systems of concepts, laws and models. Models idealise: a frictionless plane does not exist, yet it helps derive predictions.

sections.heading: Realism and observation
sections.text: Scientific realism holds that successful theories are approximately true and that unobservable entities such as electrons exist. Instrumentalism treats theories as useful instruments for prediction and stays neutral about unobservables. Bas van Fraassen’s constructive empiricism says we should accept a theory as empirically adequate, meaning it saves the observable phenomena. Theory-ladenness is the claim that observation is shaped by concepts and background theory: what a microscopist sees depends on training and expectations. This challenges the idea of neutral data.

sections.heading: Risk and ethics
sections.text: Inductive risk is the chance of error when accepting or rejecting a hypothesis. Richard Rudner argued that because scientists must decide, non-epistemic values can enter. Suppose a trial finds 12 of 20 patients improve on a new drug and 9 of 20 on standard care. The 15 percentage point difference may be chance. Calling the drug effective risks side effects; waiting risks preventable harm. Research ethics requires honesty, consent, confidentiality, animal care, credit and reporting of negative results. Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism are serious misconduct.

keyPoints: Demarcation asks what makes a claim scientific; Popper’s falsifiability is influential but not universally accepted.
Hempel’s covering-law model explains by deduction from laws and initial conditions; mechanistic accounts add causal detail.
Scientific realism affirms unobservable entities; instrumentalism treats theories as predictive instruments, and constructive empiricism accepts theories only as empirically adequate.
Theory-ladenness says observation depends on concepts and background theory, so data are not wholly neutral.
Inductive risk means accepting or rejecting a hypothesis can cause error and harm, so values can enter scientific judgement.
Research ethics requires honesty, consent, confidentiality, animal welfare, fair credit and reporting negative results.

en.title: Philosophy of Law
en.short: Natural law, legal positivism, legal realism, the Hart-Fuller debate and Dworkin on rights.

sections.heading: Three schools
sections.text:
Natural law holds that a law’s validity depends on its moral content: a deeply unjust rule is not truly law. Thomas Aquinas is the classic source. Legal positivism holds that law is a social fact, identified by its source, such as enactment or precedent, not by its merit. John Austin treated law as a sovereign’s command; H. L. A. Hart (The Concept of Law, 1961) replaced this with rules and a rule of recognition, the test officials use to identify valid law.

Legal realism says law is what courts do; Oliver Wendell Holmes called it a prediction of what courts will decide.

sections.heading: Hart and Fuller
sections.text:
The Hart-Fuller debate began in the Harvard Law Review in 1958. Hart defended the separation of law and morals: whether a rule is law is one question, whether it is just is another. Fuller replied that law has an inner morality: it must be public, general, clear, prospective, consistent, possible to obey, stable and applied as stated.

In the grudge informer case, a post-war German court punished a woman who had denounced her husband under Nazi statutes. Hart said this needed a retrospective law; Fuller said those statutes were not law at all.

sections.heading: Dworkin’s rights thesis
sections.text:
Ronald Dworkin (Taking Rights Seriously, 1977) rejected the model of rules. Law also contains principles, such as that no one may profit from his own wrong, which he drew from Riggs v Palmer (1889), where a murderer was denied his inheritance. Principles have weight rather than all-or-nothing application.

Dworkin argued that people have rights against the state, rights that trump collective goals, and that judges should interpret law as integrity, treating the law as one coherent scheme of principle.

sections.heading: Law and justice
sections.text:
Concrete legal rules differ by country: marriage, land, criminal procedure and constitutional review are settled by each state’s own law. Philosophy asks what makes a rule valid, when disobedience is justified, and what justice requires.

Legal rules vary; the arguments about their moral standing do not.

keyPoints: Natural law ties legal validity to moral content; legal positivism ties it to a social source.
Hart defended the separation of law and morals; Fuller argued that law has an inner morality.
Legal realists study what courts actually decide, not only what statutes say.
Dworkin argued that principles, not only rules, guide judges, and that rights trump collective goals.
The grudge informer case shows how the Hart-Fuller debate bears on unjust laws.
Concrete legal rules differ by country; the philosophical arguments about validity and justice do not.

en.title: Philosophy of Language: Meaning, Truth and Use
en.short: Frege, Tarski and Davidson on meaning and truth; speech acts, implicature, presupposition, vagueness, translation.

sections.heading: Sense and reference
sections.text:
Frege distinguished sense (Sinn), the mode of presentation, from reference (Bedeutung), the object. “The morning star” and “the evening star” have different senses but the same reference, Venus.

An analytic truth is true by meaning alone, such as “All bachelors are unmarried”; a synthetic truth depends on the world, such as “This bachelor is tall”. Frege treated truth as primitive. Quine later challenged the distinction.

sections.heading: Truth and meaning
sections.text:
Tarski defined truth for formal languages using an object language and a metalanguage. His schema: “Snow is white” is true if and only if snow is white. Truth is defined through satisfaction, relating formulas to objects.

Davidson used this for meaning: a theory of meaning should give truth conditions for every sentence. Interpretation also assumes speakers are largely rational and correct, the principle of charity. Critics say truth conditions miss use and context.

sections.heading: Speech and implication
sections.text:
Austin and Searle’s speech act theory separates locutionary acts (saying), illocutionary acts (promising, warning, asking) and perlocutionary effects (persuading). “I promise to come” makes a promise.

Grice distinguished speaker meaning from sentence meaning. Conversational implicature is inferred beyond what is said: if A asks “Is the seminar at nine?” and B says “The bus is on strike”, B implies that A may be late. Grice used the cooperative principle and maxims. A presupposition is a background assumption, as in “The king of France is bald”; it usually survives negation, but context affects it.

sections.heading: Vagueness and translation
sections.text:
Vagueness is the presence of borderline cases. “Heap” is vague: removing one grain seems not to stop a heap, yet repeated removal gives a non-heap. This is the sorites paradox. Epistemicists say there is a sharp boundary we cannot know; supervaluationists say a sentence is true when all admissible sharpenings make it true.

Quine’s indeterminacy of translation says rival manuals can fit all evidence while disagreeing about meaning. Hearing “gavagai” as a rabbit passes, “rabbit”, “rabbit stage” and “undetached rabbit parts” may all fit. Meaning is not determinate.

keyPoints: Frege separates sense, the mode of presentation, from reference, the object.
An analytic truth is true by meaning alone; a synthetic truth depends on the world.
Tarski defines truth for formal languages, and Davidson links meaning to truth conditions.
