Speech act theory distinguishes locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary acts.
Gricean implicature is meaning inferred beyond what is said, guided by the cooperative principle.
Presuppositions are background assumptions; vagueness and Quine’s indeterminacy show limits of determinate meaning.

en.title: Research Methods and the Philosophy Essay
en.short: Choosing a question, reading literature, structuring essays, citation and objections.

sections.heading: From topic to question
sections.text: Start with an area you can defend, then narrow it to a question with clear scope and more than one reasonable answer. A philosophical question asks whether something is true, justified, right or coherent, or what a concept means; it is not a request for a report. Amina’s title “Is free speech good?” is too broad. A workable question is “Should a public university in Nigeria punish students for offensive social media posts about staff?” It names a decision, a setting and a limit. Check that sources exist and fit the word count.

sections.heading: Reading and review
sections.text: Search the library catalogue, subject databases and philosophy bibliographies such as PhilPapers. Use keywords, then follow citations backward to the sources a text uses and forward to later works that cite it. Read the abstract, introduction and conclusion first; then read the whole text and note its claim, reasons, objections and reply. A literature review is not a list of summaries. It maps the main positions, shows where they conflict and identifies the gap your essay addresses. Record every source and page number.

sections.heading: Structuring the essay
sections.text: An argumentative essay has an introduction, body and conclusion. The introduction states the question, your thesis (the central claim) and a short plan. Each body paragraph gives one reason, explains it and links it to the thesis. State the strongest objection fairly, then reply: concede what is true, reject what is false and explain why. A dissertation chapter does the same: question, review of the debate, your argument, objections and replies, conclusion.

sections.heading: Citation and honesty
sections.text: A citation is a reference that lets a reader find the source. Cite every borrowed idea, quotation and fact. Use the style your department requires, such as Harvard, APA or Chicago, consistently. Academic honesty means giving credit and never presenting another person’s work or words as your own. Plagiarism includes copying, uncited paraphrase and submitting work written by someone else. Keep drafts and notes. When answering an objection, state the critic’s point accurately before evaluating it.

keyPoints: Narrow a broad interest into a contestable philosophical question with a clear scope.
Search library databases and philosophy bibliographies, then read for claim, reasons, objections and reply.
A literature review maps positions and identifies the gap; it is not a list of summaries.
State your thesis early and give one reason per body paragraph.
Present the strongest objection fairly and reply by conceding, rejecting or qualifying.
Cite every borrowed idea in the required style and keep notes to avoid plagiarism.

en.title: African Philosophy in the Modern World
en.short: Colonial discourse, Négritude, liberation, postcolonial thought, development ethics, rights and environment.
keywords: african charter on human and peoples’ rights

sections.heading: Colonialism and Eurocentrism
sections.text: Colonial rule did more than draw borders. It extracted land and labour, ranked races, and taught that European knowledge was universal. Eurocentrism is the habit of treating Europe as the centre and measure of humanity. Colonial discourse means the ways colonisers represented colonised peoples in speech, writing and images. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) studied Western representations of the East. Critics warn that discourse analysis can miss African agency and material exploitation; defenders say it exposes how power works through knowledge.

sections.heading: Négritude and liberation
sections.text: Négritude was a literary and philosophical movement of the 1930s. Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon-Gontran Damas affirmed Black identity and culture against colonial racism. Critics said it risked defining Blackness by contrast with Europe. Philosophy of liberation asks how thought can serve freedom from political, economic and cultural domination. Frantz Fanon analysed racial alienation and the psychology of colonial rule. Liberation is not only independence; it also concerns language, education and self-respect.

sections.heading: Postcolonial thought
sections.text: Postcolonial thought studies the legacies of empire after independence. It asks how colonial categories shape identity, language, borders and knowledge. Edward Said, Gayatri Spivak and Homi Bhabha are influential. African examples include Frantz Fanon and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, whose Decolonising the Mind (1986) argues that language is central to culture and power. The field is not one school; some stress representation, others material inequality.

sections.heading: Development, rights, environment
sections.text: Development ethics asks what development is for, who decides, and whether growth measures well-being. A mining company may offer a village money for land; ethical questions include consent, shared benefit and access to water. Ubuntu, a southern African relational ethic, holds that persons are formed through community. The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, adopted by the Organisation of African Unity in 1981, includes individual rights, peoples’ rights and duties. Scholars disagree on whether it expresses a distinctively African view. On environment, African thinkers draw on stewardship, communal land and environmental justice, but no single view represents the continent.

keyPoints: Eurocentrism treats Europe as the centre and measure of humanity.
Colonial discourse analysis studies how colonial power works through representations and knowledge.
Négritude, associated with Césaire, Senghor and Damas, affirmed Black identity against colonial racism.
Philosophy of liberation and postcolonial thought examine political, cultural and psychological legacies of empire.
Development ethics asks who benefits from development and whether people consent.
The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (adopted 1981) includes individual rights, peoples’ rights and duties; African views on rights and environment are plural.

en.title: Advanced Metaphysics and Mind
en.short: Modality, grounding, causal powers, the hard problem and panpsychism at research level.

sections.heading: Modality and worlds
sections.text: Modality concerns necessity, possibility and impossibility. Possible worlds are total ways things could be. David Lewis held that they are concrete universes; ersatzists treat them as abstract representations. Recent papers ask whether worlds can explain modal knowledge or only restate it, and whether impossible worlds are needed for hyperintensional contexts, where logically equivalent claims differ in meaning. Assess papers by asking what work worlds do and whether a cheaper account exists.

sections.heading: Grounding and fundamentality
sections.text: Grounding is a non-causal explanatory relation: one fact holds in virtue of another. Fundamentality asks what is basic, not derived. Kit Fine and Jonathan Schaffer treat grounding as primitive and use it to order reality; others reduce it to essence or truthmaking. Debates concern well-foundedness, whether every chain ends, and whether the basic level is one thing or many. A concrete case: a set’s existence may be grounded in its members, while the members are not grounded in the set. Check that grounding is not circular, one-way and transitive.

sections.heading: Causation and powers
sections.text: Humeans analyse causation through regularities or counterfactuals; interventionists say X causes Y if an ideal intervention on X changes Y. Anti-Humeans posit causal powers: dispositions grounded in intrinsic properties. The debate turns on whether powers explain regularities or merely label them. Case: a glass breaks when struck. Its structure disposes it to break, but the striking is the trigger. A powers theorist says the disposition is real; a Humean says the pattern is all. Recent work tests whether powers can handle prevention, omission and probabilistic causation.

sections.heading: Hard problem and panpsychism
sections.text: David Chalmers’s hard problem asks why physical processing is accompanied by experience, not just function. Panpsychism holds that experience, or proto-experience, is fundamental in matter. Its main difficulty is the combination problem: how micro-experiences unite into one subject. Illusionism denies phenomenal consciousness; higher-order theories and integrated information theory offer alternatives. Recent papers assess combination, panpsychist causation and whether the view is testable. Read them by separating the explanatory gap from the metaphysical conclusion.

keyPoints: Possible worlds are tools for modelling modality, but their ontology remains disputed.
Grounding is a non-causal explanatory relation, and fundamentality concerns what is basic.
Humean and powers accounts disagree over whether causation is pattern or real disposition.
The hard problem asks why physical processing is accompanied by experience.
Panpsychism treats experience as fundamental but faces the combination problem.
When assessing recent papers, separate explanatory gaps from metaphysical conclusions and check the argument’s assumptions.

en.title: Advanced Epistemology and Ethics: Testimony, Injustice and Moral Realism
en.short: Social epistemology, testimony, epistemic injustice, virtue epistemology, moral realism and responsibility.

sections.heading: Knowledge as social
sections.text: Social epistemology studies how knowledge depends on other people, institutions and shared practices. Testimony is knowledge gained from what others say or write. The live argument is between reductionists, who demand independent evidence for each speaker, and anti-reductionists, who treat testimony as a basic source unless there is reason to doubt. Ask which view explains ordinary learning without making it impossible. A student trusts a lecturer’s citation; if she checks every claim, inquiry stalls, but unchecked trust spreads error.

sections.heading: Injustice and virtue
sections.text: Miranda Fricker’s epistemic injustice names wrongs done to people as knowers. Testimonial injustice is undue discounting of a speaker because of prejudice. Hermeneutical injustice is a gap in shared concepts that leaves experience hard to understand. Virtue epistemology asks what intellectual character makes good inquiry: open-mindedness, honesty, care in evidence gathering. Evaluate the argument that virtue talk adds nothing beyond reliable belief-forming processes.

sections.heading: Realism or construction
sections.text: Moral realism holds that some moral claims are true independently of what anyone thinks. Constructivism replies that moral truths are built by practical reason, agreement or a procedure, not discovered as mind-independent facts. The argument to test is whether constructivism can explain moral objectivity without realism. If a procedure can license any outcome, it may fail; if it cannot, realism may seem unnecessary.

sections.heading: Responsibility
sections.text: Moral responsibility asks when blame or praise is fair. Standard conditions are control and knowledge: the agent could have acted otherwise and understood the act. A case: Amina, a nurse, follows a wrong dosage written by a doctor; is she responsible? The answer depends on her role, knowledge and ability to question. Evaluate whether responsibility is about choice, social expectations or reactive attitudes, feelings such as resentment and gratitude directed at people for what they do.

keyPoints: Social epistemology treats testimony as a contested source of knowledge, not a mere convenience.
Reductionists demand independent evidence; anti-reductionists accept testimony as basic unless there is reason to doubt.
Fricker distinguishes testimonial injustice from hermeneutical injustice.
Virtue epistemology evaluates intellectual character and its role in reliable inquiry.
Moral realism and constructivism disagree about the source of moral truth, not always about particular judgments.
Moral responsibility normally requires control and knowledge, but social role can affect blame.

en.title: Dissertation Research Design and Writing in Philosophy
en.short: Covers proposal, literature search, thesis, chapter plan, drafting, integrity, citation and defence.

sections.heading: Proposal and supervisor
sections.text: A dissertation is a sustained piece of independent philosophical argument. Length and rules vary by department, so check your handbook. Begin with a short proposal: the question, why it matters, your provisional answer, main sources and a timetable. Agree the scope with your supervisor in writing. A workable topic is narrow enough to treat well and broad enough to find sources.

sections.heading: Reading and thesis
sections.text: Search steadily, not once. Use library catalogues, philosophy databases and bibliographies, then follow citations forward and backward. Keep a record of every source and note page numbers. Read primary texts and secondary works for orientation. A thesis statement is one arguable sentence your dissertation defends. Example: Amina studies communal duty and environmental care in African thought. Her thesis might be: 'Communal personhood grounds duties to future generations, but only when combined with a principle of accountability.' She tests it against objections.

sections.heading: Plan and drafting
sections.text: Turn the thesis into a chapter plan. A common shape is introduction, three or four argument chapters, and conclusion. Each chapter should answer one question and advance the overall claim. Draft early and progressively. Write the easiest chapter first if that helps, then revise. Send chapters to your supervisor on an agreed schedule. Leave time for rewriting, formatting and proofreading. Your conclusion should state what you argued, what you conceded and what remains open.

sections.heading: Integrity and defence
sections.text: Research integrity means honesty about sources, evidence and help. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words or ideas as your own, including close paraphrase without citation. Cite consistently in the style your department requires, give page numbers for quotations, and cite what you have actually read. A master’s contribution need not be a new system. It can be a clear new argument, a careful critique, a synthesis or an application. Standards vary, so ask your supervisor what originality means in your field. For the defence, prepare a summary, anticipate objections and admit limits.

keyPoints: A dissertation is sustained independent argument; length and rules vary by department, so check the handbook.
Agree a narrow, feasible topic and scope with your supervisor in writing before drafting.
A thesis statement is one arguable sentence that the whole dissertation defends.
A chapter plan should give each chapter one question and a role in the overall argument.
Cite every source consistently, give page numbers for quotations, and never present another person’s words or ideas as your own.
At master’s level, originality can be a new argument, critique, synthesis or application; ask your supervisor what your department requires.

en.title: Frontier Topic: Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence and Mind
en.short: Machine consciousness, autonomous systems ethics, algorithmic fairness and the epistemology of large models.

sections.heading: Consciousness and machines
sections.text:
Turing (1950) replaced 'can machines think?' with an imitation game: can a machine’s replies pass as a person’s? Searle’s Chinese Room (1980) answers that rule-governed symbol manipulation is not understanding. Chalmers (1995) named the hard problem: why is information processing accompanied by experience?

Block separates access consciousness, information available for reasoning and report, from phenomenal consciousness, what it is like to undergo something. Nagel (1974) holds a creature is conscious if there is something it is like to be it. Functionalists say causal roles fix mental states, so silicon could serve; biological naturalists deny it.

sections.heading: Prediction and understanding
sections.text:
A large language model is trained by next-token prediction: it learns a probability distribution over the next token given the preceding text. Accurate prediction does not by itself settle understanding. Bender and Koller (2020) argue that meaning needs grounding in communicative intent; others reply that sufficient structure may supply it. 'Hallucination' is a term of art for fluent output not supported by evidence.

Epistemic problems include opacity, benchmark contamination (test items leaking into training data) and over-trust in machine testimony.

sections.heading: Fairness and accountability
sections.text:
Fairness metrics conflict. Chouldechova (2017) and Kleinberg and colleagues (2016) show that when base rates (overall outcome rates) differ between groups, a risk score cannot be calibrated within each group (a given score corresponds to the same actual risk in each group) and also have equal false positive and false negative rates. ProPublica’s 2016 analysis of the COMPAS recidivism tool reported a higher false positive rate for Black defendants (labelled high risk but did not reoffend); the vendor disputed the reading. Both claims can be true at once.

Matthias (2004) named the responsibility gap: autonomous systems may act where no person meets ordinary conditions of liability. Proposed answers: meaningful human control, audit, strict liability, insurance.

sections.heading: Rules and agency
sections.text:
The EU AI Act (2024) sorts systems by risk and bans some uses; national data protection laws, such as Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023, also apply. Details and timelines change, so check current official texts.

If agency requires reasons-responsive self-control, delegating decisions to opaque systems thins accountability without erasing it.

keyPoints: The Turing test measures indistinguishability in conversation, not inner experience.
Searle argues that symbol manipulation alone does not give understanding.
Access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness are distinct notions.
Next-token prediction is statistical; whether it yields understanding is disputed.
Fairness metrics can conflict: calibration and equal error rates may not both hold when base rates differ.
The responsibility gap arises when autonomous systems act and no person is plainly liable.
